title: Tunisia Climate Analysis: A Comparative Study
text:
This capstone project presents a comprehensive analysis of climate patterns across three Tunisian cities: Bizerte, Sousse, and Kef. Using hourly environmental sensor data, we investigate temperature trends, humidity patterns, wind characteristics, and solar radiation levels to understand regional climate variations and identify key meteorological patterns.






NoteKey Findings




Temperature variations reveal distinct climatic zones
Coastal cities show higher humidity levels
Clear diurnal and seasonal patterns identified
Solar radiation patterns differ significantly by location
crumbs: Tunisia Climate Analysis: A Comparative Study

text:
1. Introduction

1.1 Background
Climate analysis is essential for understanding regional weather patterns, planning agricultural activities, and assessing environmental conditions. Tunisia’s diverse geography—from Mediterranean coastal regions to inland continental areas—creates varied climatic conditions that significantly impact local ecosystems and human activities.


1.2 Research Objectives
This study aims to:

Analyze temperature patterns across three distinct Tunisian cities
Compare humidity levels and their seasonal variations
Investigate wind characteristics and their relationship with other variables
Examine solar radiation patterns and their implications
Identify key climate indicators for each location



1.3 Study Locations
Our analysis focuses on three cities representing different climatic regions:

Bizerte - Northern coastal city on the Mediterranean
Sousse - Eastern coastal city with tourist significance
Kef - Inland mountainous region in the northwest

2. Dataset Description

2.1 Data Source
The dataset originates from the Tunisian Open Data Portal (https://catalog.data.gov.tn), specifically from the “Capteur d’environnement de la station climatique” (Environmental Climate Station Sensors) program.


2.2 Data Structure


Code
```{r data-overview}
# Display data structure
cat("Dataset Dimensions:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Observations: %s\n", format(nrow(climate_data), big.mark = ",")))
cat(sprintf("  Variables: %d\n", ncol(climate_data)))
cat(sprintf("  Cities: %d\n", n_distinct(climate_data$city)))
cat(sprintf("  Date Range: %s to %s\n", 
            min(climate_data$date), 
            max(climate_data$date)))
```


Dataset Dimensions:
  Observations: 1,073
  Variables: 17
  Cities: 3
  Date Range: NA to NA

3. Methodology

3.1 Data Collection
Data was collected from environmental sensors at three weather stations, recording hourly measurements throughout the study period.


3.2 Data Processing Pipeline



DATA PROCESSING WORKFLOW
========================

1. RAW DATA LOADING
   ↓
   • Load CSV files from three cities
   • Combine into single dataset
   ↓
2. DATA CLEANING
   ↓
   • Parse datetime stamps
   • Transform from long to wide format
   • Handle missing values
   • Validate data quality
   ↓
3. EXPLORATORY ANALYSIS
   ↓
   • Statistical summaries
   • Correlation analysis
   • Pattern identification
   ↓
4. VISUALIZATION
   ↓
   • Time series plots
   • Distribution analysis
   • Comparative visualizations
   ↓
5. INTERPRETATION & REPORTING




3.3 Statistical Methods
Our analysis employs:

Descriptive statistics (mean, median, SD, quartiles)
Time series analysis (trends, seasonality)
Correlation analysis (Pearson correlation)
Comparative analysis (ANOVA, distribution comparison)
Extreme value analysis (min/max events)

4. Data Cleaning

4.1 Data Quality Assessment


Code
```{r data-quality}
# Missing values summary
missing_summary <- climate_data %>%
  summarise(across(
    c(temperature, humidity, wind_speed, dew_point, solar_radiation),
    ~sum(is.na(.)),
    .names = "missing_{.col}"
  ))

# Quality flags
quality_summary <- climate_data %>%
  count(quality_flag) %>%
  mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))

quality_summary %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Data Quality Flags") %>%
  cols_label(
    quality_flag = "Quality Status",
    n = "Count",
    percentage = "Percentage (%)"
  ) %>%
  opt_stylize(style = 6, color = "green")
```

4.2 Data Transformations
Key transformations applied:

DateTime parsing: Converted string timestamps to proper datetime objects
Wide format transformation: Pivoted from long to wide format for easier analysis
Feature engineering: Created time-based features (hour, day, month, season)
Outlier detection: Flagged unrealistic values for review

8. Interpretation

8.1 Geographic Influences
The analysis reveals strong geographic influences on climate patterns:

Coastal Effect: Bizerte and Sousse exhibit maritime climate characteristics with higher humidity and more moderate temperatures
Altitude Impact: Kef’s inland and elevated position results in greater temperature variability and lower humidity
Mediterranean Influence: All locations show typical Mediterranean seasonal patterns

For Energy: - Solar radiation patterns inform renewable energy potential - Wind speed data relevant for wind energy assessment

title: Tunisia Climate Analysis: A Comparative Study
text:
9. Conclusions

9.1 Summary of Findings

Temperature Patterns

Clear temperature gradients from coast to inland
Seasonal variations follow Mediterranean patterns
Diurnal cycles show consistent patterns across cities

Humidity Analysis

Coastal cities maintain higher humidity levels
Inverse relationship with temperature observed
Seasonal humidity variations identified

Wind Characteristics

Variable wind patterns across locations
Coastal areas experience different wind regimes
Clear temporal patterns in wind speed

Solar Radiation

Consistent diurnal patterns across all cities
Seasonal variations in solar intensity
Minimal inter-city differences in solar patterns




9.2 Study Limitations

Data limited to specific time period
Sensor accuracy not independently verified
Some missing data points in certain periods
Limited to three locations



9.3 Future Research Directions

Extend analysis to include more cities
Incorporate longer time series for trend analysis
Add climate change impact assessment
Develop predictive models for forecasting

title: About This Project
text:
Reproducibility Statement
This entire analysis is reproducible. All code, data processing steps, and visualizations can be regenerated by:

Cloning the repository
Installing required R packages
Running the analysis scripts in order
Rendering the Quarto website

For detailed instructions, see the README.md in the project repository.
